citation: Lauderdale DS, Knutson KL, Yan LL, Liu K, Rathouz PJ. Self-reported and measured sleep duration: how similar are they? Epidemiology. 2008;19(6):838-845.
your_quote: For habitual sleep in wave 1, the bias at the mean of 6 hours measured sleep was 0.80 hours (48 minutes), with subjective reports longer than measured sleep (table 2). || Table 2 row: Full Sample (n=647) | 0.70 | 0.80 | 0.71, 0.88 | 0.51 | 0.35, 0.67 | 0.20 | 0.11, 0.30 | 6.29 | 7.31
your_note: Bias is the regression intercept of self-reported habitual sleep on 3-night actigraphy, evaluated at the sample mean of 6 h measured sleep. Value 0.80 h, sign already matches the target unit (self-report longer than actigraphy). SE from the Table 2 95% CI: (0.88 - 0.71)/3.92 = 0.0434. n = 647 wave-1 participants with adequate 3-night actigraphy (669 consented, 19 dropped for inadequate data). Alternative numbers in the paper that do NOT match this target: single-night bias 0.63 h (wave 2, n = 615) and the sensitivity-analysis bias 0.86 h after excluding 216 records. RoB coded na because the target is a descriptive measurement-validity parameter, not a comparative effect estimate; if a judgement is forced, moderate (single cohort, single site, only 3 nights treated as a random sample of 30).

citation: Markwald RR, Melanson EL, Smith MR, Higgins J, Perreault L, Eckel RH, Wright KP Jr. Impact of insufficient sleep on total daily energy expenditure, food intake, and weight gain. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA. 2013;110(14):5695-5700.
your_quote: We also found that transitioning from an insufficient to adequate/recovery sleep schedule decreased energy intake, especially of fats and carbohydrates, and led to −0.03 ± 0.50 kg weight loss.
your_note: Value as reported: -0.03 kg body-weight change during the 9-h adequate/recovery condition in the participants who crossed over from the 5-h to the 9-h condition. Reported dispersion is an SD (0.50 kg); SE = 0.50/sqrt(8) = 0.1768, using n = 8 because condition-by-order planned comparisons were run on the order subgroups (Fig. 2 legend: 'planned comparisons for condition by order (Right, n = 8 each order, one-tailed dependent t tests)'). Negative sign = weight loss once sleep was normalised. Design: 14-15 d inpatient counterbalanced crossover with 5-h vs 9-h sleep opportunities; rct_crossover would be an equally defensible label. RoB some_concerns: n = 8 for this specific order subgroup, ad libitum food intake, and the estimate is a secondary order-stratified comparison.

citation: Daghlas I, Lane JM, Saxena R, Vetter C. Genetically Proxied Diurnal Preference, Sleep Timing, and Risk of Major Depressive Disorder. JAMA Psychiatry. 2021 Aug 1;78(8):903-910.
your_quote: Results were similar when considering the subset of MDD cases in the PGC meta-analysis (n = 45 369 affected individuals and 97 250 control participants; OR, 0.73 [95% CI, 0.54-1.00]; P = .05) and the UKB alone (n = 133 769 affected individuals and 208 111 control participants; OR, 0.75 [95% CI, 0.60-0.92]; P = .007; Figure 3).
your_note: Stringently defined MDD = the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium case definition (interviewer/clinician ascertained), reported separately from the broader UK Biobank definition. Conversion: log_or = ln(0.73) = -0.31471; SE = (ln(1.00) - ln(0.54))/3.92 = 0.15719 (SE from the p = .05 alone would be ~0.161, consistent). n = 45,369 cases + 97,250 controls = 142,619. Sign: negative = 1 h EARLIER genetically proxied sleep midpoint is associated with lower MDD odds, i.e. the sign follows the target unit as written. The task's global convention (positive = elevated risk with short sleep) is not applicable here because the exposure is sleep timing/diurnal preference, not sleep duration. RoB some_concerns: standard two-sample MR caveats (pleiotropy, linear approximation around the population mean, sleep midpoint not diary-confirmed); Egger intercept test was null.

citation: Beals JW, Smith GI, Farabi SS, Patterson BW, Lucey BP, Broussard JL, Wright KP Jr, Klein S. Sleep extension improves sleep health but not insulin sensitivity in people with overweight or obesity who maintain habitual short sleep schedules. Diabetes Care. 2026;49(5):740-745.
target_unit: hours/night of sleep gained, extension group minus control group
your_quote: Table 1, Daily total sleep time (h) | 6.1 ± 0.5 | 6.1 ± 0.5 | 0.0 (−0.2, 0.2) | 5.8 ± 0.5 | 6.9 ± 0.7 | 1.1 (0.8, 1.4) | <0.001 || Abstract: Time in bed and sleep duration increased more in the ES group (1.3 ± 0.6 and 1.1 ± 0.5 h/night) than in the HS group (0.3 ± 0.8 and 0.0 ± 0.4 h/night).
your_note: Actigraphy total sleep time: extension (ES) group within-group change +1.1 h/night (95% CI 0.8, 1.4); habitual-sleep (HS) control change 0.0 h/night (95% CI -0.2, 0.2). Extension minus control = 1.1 - 0.0 = 1.1 h/night. SE: SE_ES = (1.4-0.8)/3.92 = 0.15306, SE_HS = (0.2-(-0.2))/3.92 = 0.10204, SE_diff = sqrt(0.15306^2 + 0.10204^2) = 0.18396 (treats the two parallel arms as independent). n = 29 completers (HS 15, ES 14; 31 randomised, 1 withdrawal per arm). Intervention length described as ~6 weeks / 5.5 weeks, consistent with the 42-day target. RoB some_concerns: small unblinded behavioural trial, predominantly women, and half the ES group never reached >=7 h/night; the achieved-exposure outcome itself is objectively measured.

citation: Zitting KM, Munch MY, Cain SW, Wang W, Wong A, Ronda JM, Aeschbach D, Czeisler CA, Duffy JF. Young adults are more vulnerable to chronic sleep deficiency and recurrent circadian disruption than older adults. Sci Rep. 2018;8(1):11052.
your_quote: Young participants were also significantly more likely to have at least one inadvertent sleep during their PVTs than were older participants [χ² (1, N = 23) = 5.49, p = 0.0191].
your_note: The only effect-size-convertible statistic the paper reports for inadvertent sleep during PVTs as a function of age is this 2x2 chi-square. Conversion: phi = sqrt(5.49/23) = 0.48857; Cohen's d = 2*phi/sqrt(1-phi^2) = 1.11988; J = 1 - 3/(4*(23-2)-1) = 0.96386; Hedges g = 1.07941. SE_d = sqrt(N/(n1*n2) + d^2/(2(N-2))) = sqrt(23/(12*11) + 1.11988^2/42) = 0.45178; SE_g = J*SE_d = 0.43545 (the alternative g/sqrt(chi2) = 0.4607 is very close). n = 23 (12 young, 11 older; the older group has n = 11 for PVT measures). SIGN IS CONVENTION-DEPENDENT and a likely disagreement source: the contrast is young vs older adults, not restricted vs rested, so the task's 'negative = worse under restriction' rule does not map directly. I signed it negative because the group the paper identifies as more vulnerable to the 5.6 h/24 h restriction (young adults) had the worse outcome (more inadvertent sleep); magnitude is 1.08 either way. Also note the chi-square is on the dichotomy 'at least one inadvertent sleep during PVTs', whereas the mixed-model FD-cycle-by-age interaction (F2,11310 = 19.61, p < 0.0001) is a different, non-convertible expression of the same moderation. RoB moderate: the age contrast is a non-randomised between-group comparison inside a well-controlled 21-day inpatient CSR/forced-desynchrony protocol; EEG/EOG available for only ~64% of scheduled wake.

citation: Lloyd-Jones DM, Leip EP, Larson MG, D'Agostino RB, Beiser A, Wilson PW, Wolf PA, Levy D. Prediction of lifetime risk for cardiovascular disease by risk factor burden at 50 years of age. Circulation. 2006;113(6):791-798.
target_unit: probability of first atherosclerotic CVD event from exact age 50 to age 95
your_quote: We followed up 3564 men and 4362 women for 111,777 person-years; 1757 had CVD events and 1641 died free of CVD. At 50 years of age, lifetime risks were 51.7% (95% CI, 49.3 to 54.2) for men and 39.2% (95% CI, 37.0 to 41.4) for women, with median survivals of 30 and 36 years, respectively.
your_note: Lifetime risk of first atherosclerotic CVD event (MI, coronary insufficiency, angina, stroke, claudication) from age 50 to age 95 in Framingham men, with death free of CVD treated as a competing event - exactly the target construct. Probability = 51.7/100 = 0.517; SE = (0.542 - 0.493)/3.92 = 0.0125. n = 3,564 men free of CVD at age 50. Retrieved from the PubMed abstract (efetch); the full text was paywalled, but the abstract states the estimate, CI and denominators. RoB na: competing-risk life-table estimate in a single, largely white community cohort - generalisability rather than internal bias is the limitation.

citation: Meredith-Jones KA, Haszard JJ, Graham-DeMello A, Campbell A, Stewart T, Galland BC, Cox A, Kennedy G, Duncan S, Taylor RW. Validation of actigraphy sleep metrics in children aged 8 to 16 years: considerations for device type, placement and algorithms. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act. 2024;21(1):40.
target_unit: proportion of time in bed spent asleep
your_quote: Sleep efficiency TIB (%) | PSG | n = 114 | 89.1 (12.5) | Reference
your_note: Home PSG reference value for sleep efficiency defined as TST/TIB (the paper's 'Sleep efficiency-TIB'), from the Actigraph comparison table: 89.1% (SD 12.5), n = 114, so probability = 0.891. SE of the mean = 12.5/sqrt(114) = 1.171% = 0.01171. Ambiguity: the parallel Axivity table gives PSG Sleep efficiency TIB = 88.8% (SD 9.6), n = 116, because only participants with complete data for each device set are included; and the paper's other definition, Sleep efficiency-SPT, is 95.0% (4.1). The target explicitly specifies TST/TIB, so 0.891 is the matching value; an extractor who used the Axivity table would report 0.888, or 0.950 if they took the SPT definition. RoB na: single-night PSG descriptive reference value in a validation study.

citation: Campbell IG, Kurinec CA, Zhang ZY, Cruz-Basilio A, Figueroa JG, Bottom VB, Feinberg I. Sleep restriction and age effects on distinct aspects of cognition in adolescents. Sleep. 2024;47(12):zsae216.
target_unit: dB of PVT log signal-to-noise ratio
your_quote: As TIB was decreased from 10 to 8.5 hours LSNR decreased (t3333 = 4.65, p < .0001) by 0.33 ± 0.07 dB (estimate ± SE), which is equivalent to a 7.3% reduction in the fidelity of information processing.
your_note: Exactly the specified contrast (8.5 h vs 10 h TIB for four consecutive nights). Value signed negative because LSNR decreased, i.e. worse vigilant attention under the shorter TIB. SE = 0.07 dB as published (estimate +/- SE); consistent with the reported t = 4.65 (0.33/0.07 = 4.71). n = 159 participants contributing (younger cohort 77 + older cohort 82); the mixed model has 3,333 residual df because each participant contributed up to 4 PVTs per condition per year across multiple years. The further 8.5 -> 7 h step was 0.44 +/- 0.07 dB, which is a different contrast. RoB low: within-subject randomised-order TIB conditions, actigraphy/diary-verified schedules, urine screening for caffeine/drugs.

citation: Sambou ML, Zhao X, Hong T, Wang N, Dai J. Associations between sleep-behavioral traits and healthspan: A one-sample Mendelian randomization study based on 388,909 participants of the UK-Biobank. J Affect Disord. 2024 Apr 1;350:854-862.
your_quote: In IPTW, we observed a decreased risk of terminated healthspan for healthy sleep behaviors such as 'sleep duration 7-8h/d' (Hazard ratio, HR = 0.93; 95 % confidence interval, CI: 0.92-0.96; P < 0.001)
your_note: The paper's observational IPTW estimate is reported for the HEALTHY exposure category (self-reported sleep duration 7-8 h/d, midpoint 7.5 h, matching the target referent) versus everyone else. To express it on the target's direction (elevated risk with short sleep) I inverted: log_hr = -ln(0.93) = 0.07257; SE = (ln(0.96) - ln(0.92))/3.92 = 0.01086 (invariant under inversion). SPEC CONCERN: the comparison group in the paper pools short AND long sleepers, so this is 'abnormal sleep duration vs 7-8 h', not a pure short-sleep contrast; the paper (as far as the abstract shows) does not report a short-sleep-specific IPTW HR. Access limitation: the article is paywalled (Elsevier page returned a JS shell, Unpaywall reports is_oa = false), so only the PubMed abstract could be read and the category definitions in the full text could not be checked. n = 388,909 UK Biobank participants for the overall analysis. The companion MR estimate for healthy sleep duration was OR 0.98 (0.97-1.00) - a different quantity from the requested observational IPTW HR. RoB moderate: self-reported categorical exposure, IPTW-adjusted observational analysis, healthy-volunteer cohort.

citation: Prather AA, Janicki-Deverts D, Hall MH, Cohen S. Behaviorally Assessed Sleep and Susceptibility to the Common Cold. Sleep. 2015;38(9):1353-1359.
your_quote: As illustrated in Figure 1, the predictive influence of sleep duration on cold susceptibility indicates a threshold effect at 6 or fewer hours of sleep (< 5 h, OR = 4.50; 95% CI 1.08–18.69; 5–6 h, OR = 4.24; 95% CI 1.08–16.71; 6.01–7 h, OR = 1.66; 95% CI 0.40–6.95; > 7 h, 1 [reference]).
your_note: Outcome is the biologically verified clinical cold (infection plus objective illness criteria: adjusted mucus weight >= 10 g or nasal clearance time >= 35 min). Contrast chosen: actigraphic sleep < 5 h vs > 7 h, which matches the target dose 4.5 h vs referent 7.6 h as category midpoints. Conversion: log_or = ln(4.50) = 1.50408; SE = (ln(18.69) - ln(1.08))/3.92 = 0.72730. n = 164 participants who were quarantined and challenged with rhinovirus. Adjacent category 5-6 h (OR 4.24) is nearly identical, so category choice barely changes the estimate. Design: exposure was 7 days of wrist actigraphy before an experimental viral challenge and is observational (not randomised), so prospective_cohort_objective / T4. RoB moderate: objective exposure and hard outcome, but small n, very wide CI, and residual confounding possible despite extensive adjustment.

citation: Fryar CD, Kit B, Carroll MD, Afful J. Hypertension Prevalence, Awareness, Treatment, and Control Among Adults Age 18 and Older: United States, August 2021-August 2023. NCHS Data Brief No. 511. Hyattsville, MD: National Center for Health Statistics; 2024.
target_unit: prevalence of hypertension in US men aged 40-59
your_quote: Hypertension prevalence was higher in men than women ages 18–39 (30.0% compared with 16.4%) and 40–59 (55.9% compared with 49.0%), but the prevalence was not significantly different between men and women age 60 and older. || Table 1 row: Men ... 40–59 752 55.9 (50.6–61.1) 2.4
your_note: NHANES August 2021-August 2023 crude prevalence of hypertension (SBP >= 130 or DBP >= 80 mm Hg, or currently taking antihypertensive medication) in men aged 40-59: 55.9% -> 0.559. SE taken from Table 1 as published (2.4 percentage points -> 0.024); the tabled 95% CI (50.6-61.1) is a Korn-Graubard interval and implies a slightly larger SE of (0.611-0.506)/3.92 = 0.0268, so an extractor using the CI rule would report 0.027. n = 752 men aged 40-59 examined. Retrieved the data brief PDF text directly from the NCHS site. RoB na: nationally representative descriptive survey estimate.

citation: Depner CM, Melanson EL, Eckel RH, Snell-Bergeon JK, Perreault L, Bergman BC, Higgins JA, Guerin MK, Stothard ER, Morton SJ, Wright KP Jr. Ad libitum weekend recovery sleep fails to prevent metabolic dysregulation during a repeating pattern of insufficient sleep and weekend recovery sleep. Curr Biol. 2019;29(6):957-967.e4.
target_unit: h TST on the maximal ad-lib recovery night
your_quote: Table 1, Total Sleep Time (h), columns SD2 BL | SD3 BL | SD4 WW-1 | SD5 WW-1 | SD8 WE-Friday | SD9 WE-Saturday | SD10 WE-Sunday | SD11 WW-2: WR | 8.1±0.1 | 8.1±0.1 | 4.5±0.1 * | 4.7±0.1 * | 10.0±0.4 * | 9.2±0.5 * | 6.1±0.3 * | 4.5±0.1 *
your_note: Maximal polysomnographic TST on an ad libitum weekend recovery night in the weekend-recovery (WR) group = 10.0 h (SEM 0.4) on study day 8 (simulated Friday), against a baseline of 8.1 h (SEM 0.1), matching the target referent of 8.1 h. SE = 0.4 as published (SEM). n = 14 (WR group; 7 men, 7 women), healthy young adults (mean age 27.4 y). SPEC CONCERN about the stated 12.1 h dose: the WR weekend had an enforced minimum of 10 h time in bed with napping permitted, and the only 12.1 h figure in the paper is men-only time in bed on study day 9 (Men: 12.1 +/- 0.7 h SEM on day 9), not the TIB on the night with maximal TST. Related alternatives an extractor might have taken: men's TST on day 9 = 10.2 +/- 0.6 h, or day 9 group TST = 9.2 +/- 0.5 h. RoB some_concerns: randomised three-group inpatient protocol, but this value is a within-group descriptive mean in a small arm; design could equally be coded rct_parallel since group assignment was randomised.

citation: Sabia S, Fayosse A, Dumurgier J, van Hees VT, Paquet C, Sommerlad A, Kivimaki M, Dugravot A, Singh-Manoux A. Association of sleep duration in middle and old age with incidence of dementia. Nature Communications. 2021 Apr 20;12(1):2289.
your_quote: Further adjustment for health behaviours and cardiometabolic and mental health factors attenuated associations, but there remained an association for short sleep at 50 (hazard ratio (HR) = 1.22, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 1.01–1.48) and 60 years (HR = 1.37, 95% CI = 1.10–1.72).
your_note: Fully adjusted HR for short sleep (<= 6 h/night) versus normal sleep (7 h/night) measured at age 50, Whitehall II, mean follow-up 24.6 y. Conversion: log_hr = ln(1.22) = 0.19885; SE = (ln(1.48) - ln(1.01))/3.92 = 0.09747. Positive = elevated dementia risk with short sleep, matching the task convention. n = 7,959 participants with sleep and covariate data at age 50 (521 incident dementia cases). Other estimates in the paper that do not match this target: short sleep at age 60 (HR 1.37) and at 70 (HR 1.24), and persistent short sleep across ages (HR 1.30). RoB moderate: self-reported categorical sleep duration, occupational cohort, possible reverse causation despite long follow-up (results were robust to APOE adjustment and to excluding prior mental illness).

citation: Tort-Colet N, Stankeviciute L, Fernandez-Arcos A, Soldevila-Domenech N, Sanchez-Benavides G, Shekari M, Vallez Garcia D, Altomare D, Barkhof F, Boada M, et al. Self-reported sleep quality and longitudinal amyloid burden in clinically unimpaired adults from the AMYPAD PNHS study. Alzheimer's Research & Therapy. 2026 Apr 17;18(1).
target_unit: Centiloid per year per 1-point increase in PSQI global score
your_quote: The PSQI global score was not significantly associated with Aβ burden at baseline (β = 0.12, CI = [−0.41, 0.66], p = 0.658), and the interaction of PSQI global score with time was not significant (β = 0.04, CI = [−0.04, 0.11], p = 0.352) (Table 2).
your_note: Target quantity is the PSQI-by-time interaction in Model 1 (whole sample), i.e. Centiloid/year per 1-point higher PSQI: beta = 0.04, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.11 (Table 2 row 'PSQI x visit years | 0.04 | [-0.04, 0.11] | 0.352'). SE = (0.11 - (-0.04))/3.92 = 0.03827. n = 417 clinically unimpaired adults (336 with one and 81 with two follow-up PET scans). Positive sign = faster amyloid accumulation with worse self-reported sleep quality; the estimate is null, consistent with the '_NULL' suffix in the construct name. Note on the spec: target_scale 'per_hour_beta' is a misnomer here because the exposure is PSQI points, not hours; the target_unit text is the correct description. Do not confuse with the stratified interaction terms (grey-zone group 0.22 [0.04, 0.41]; amyloid-positive group -0.41 [-0.73, -0.10]), which are subgroup contrasts relative to the amyloid-negative group. RoB moderate: single baseline self-report exposure, multi-cohort pooling with cohort as fixed effect, no medication/lifestyle covariates.

citation: Cousins JN, Sasmita K, Chee MWL. Memory encoding is impaired after multiple nights of partial sleep restriction. Journal of Sleep Research. 2018;27(1):138-145.
your_quote: Recognition was poorer in the SR group, as evidenced by significantly lower A0 scores [t(57) = 3.459, P = 0.001; Cohen's d = 0.9] (Fig. 2c).
your_note: Quote is verbatim from the PDF text layer, in which the A-prime symbol (A') is rendered as 'A0'; the outcome is the A' discrimination index for delayed picture recognition, tested after 3 recovery nights so that it indexes encoding capacity rather than state sleepiness. Conversion: d = t*sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2) = 3.459*sqrt(1/29 + 1/30) = 0.90078 (matches the paper's reported d = 0.9); J = 1 - 3/(4*57 - 1) = 0.98678; Hedges g = 0.88887, signed NEGATIVE because recognition was worse in the sleep-restricted group. SE_d = sqrt(59/(29*30) + d^2/(2*57)) = 0.27374; SE_g = J*SE_d = 0.27012. n = 59 (SR 29 with 5 h TIB for 5 nights, control 30 with 9 h TIB). Design: randomised parallel-group in-lab protocol (Need for Sleep 3), so rct_parallel rather than the within-subject lab label. RoB some_concerns: randomised and monitored continuously, but parallel groups with n ~30, single site, adolescents only, and no blinding of participants to condition.

citation: Duraccio KM, Kaiser N, Ehsani S, Blackburn BE, Zaugg K, Ho KJ, Kelly RG, Jarrett S, Krietsch KN, Beebe DW, Jones BL. Effect of Sleep Restriction on Adolescent Cognition by Adiposity: A Randomized Crossover Trial. JAMA Neurology. 2024;81(7):712-720.
your_quote: Adolescents with overweight or obesity had poorer global cognition (mean [SD] restricted, 98.0 [2.8]; mean [SD] adequate, 103.2 [2.9]; mean difference, 5.18; P = .003), fluid cognition (mean [SD] restricted, 94.5 [3.2]; mean [SD] adequate, 102.0 [3.6]; mean difference, 7.49; P < .001), and cognitive flexibility (mean [SD] restricted, 84.8 [3.0]; mean [SD] adequate, 92.8 [3.0]; mean difference, 8.00; P < .001) scores following restricted sleep.
your_note: No Cohen's d is reported for this contrast, so it must be derived. I used the standardisation the authors themselves apply: 'As 1 SD in age-standardized scores for the National Institutes of Health toolbox is 15, the decreases observed in cognitive performance among adolescents with overweight or obesity decreased was approximately 0.35 to 0.53 SDs after 1 night of sleep restriction.' Hence d = -5.18/15 = -0.3453 (negative = worse global cognition after the 4.2 h restricted night). SE: from P = .003 with df = 56, t = 3.103, so SE of the mean difference = 5.18/3.103 = 1.669 and SE_d = 1.669/15 = 0.1113. IMPORTANT disagreement risk: the bracketed values labelled [SD] (2.8, 2.9) are model-based standard errors of the marginal means, not SDs - an SD of 2.8 is implausible on a scale whose normative SD is 15 - so treating them as SDs would give d ~ -1.8. A within-subject d_z (t/sqrt(30) = 0.57) is another possible convention. n = 30 adolescents with overweight or obesity (final sample 61; 31 healthy weight). Achieved sleep: restricted 4 h 12 min, adequate 8 h 54 min, matching the target dose/referent. RoB some_concerns: randomised single-blind crossover but at-home sleep conditions, documented order/practice effects handled by covariate adjustment, and this is a subgroup contrast from a BMI-by-condition interaction.

citation: Klerman EB, Dijk DJ. Age-related reduction in the maximal capacity for sleep - implications for insomnia. Curr Biol. 2008;18(15):1118-1123.
target_unit: h TST per 24 h at asymptote
your_quote: The asymptotic value for TST for younger subjects was 8.9 hours (C.I. 8.1-9.7 hours) (p=0.009 vs. older) and was not achieved until approximately the fifth 24-hour of extended sleep opportunity.
your_note: Model-fitted asymptote of total sleep time per 24 h in younger subjects under 16 h daily bedrest (12 h at night plus a 4 h afternoon opportunity), estimated by mixed-model exponential regression: 8.9 h. SE = 0.4 as published in the abstract and Table 1 ('8.9 +/- 0.4' s.e.m.); the CI-derived value (9.7 - 8.1)/3.92 = 0.408 agrees. n = 35 younger subjects; their habitual sleep duration was 8.5 +/- 1.0 h, matching the target referent. Two spec caveats: (1) protocol length was randomised to 3, 4 or 7 days (9 younger subjects had 7 days), so the 7-day target duration applies only to a subset while the asymptote is fitted across all; (2) the HSD-matched younger subset gives 9.2 h (8.3-10.1), which does not match 'young adults' as specified. RoB some_concerns: well-controlled inpatient protocol, but the value is an extrapolated model asymptote and the young asymptote was not reached until ~day 5.

citation: Yin J, Jin X, Shan Z, Li S, Huang H, Li P, Peng X, Peng Z, Yu K, Bao W, Yang W, Chen X, Liu L. Relationship of Sleep Duration With All-Cause Mortality and Cardiovascular Events: A Systematic Review and Dose-Response Meta-Analysis of Prospective Cohort Studies. J Am Heart Assoc. 2017 Sep 9;6(9):e005947.
your_quote: Table 2 (Association Between Sleep Duration and All-Cause Mortality, Total CVD, CHD and Stroke From Non-Linear Dose-Response Analysis): Sleep Duration | All-Cause Mortality (n=40) | Total CVD (n=26) | CHD (n=20) | Stroke (n=17) ... 6 h | 1.01 (1.00–1.01) | 1.02 (1.00–1.03) | 1.05 (1.03–1.08) | 0.99 (0.96–1.03) ... 7 h | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00
your_note: Chose the non-linear dose-response estimate for total CVD at 6 h with 7 h as the reference, which is the exact 6-h-vs-7-h contrast the target names: RR 1.02 (1.00-1.03). log_rr = ln(1.02) = 0.01980; SE = (ln(1.03) - ln(1.00))/3.92 = 0.00754. MAIN DISAGREEMENT RISK: the paper's headline linear estimate is RR 1.06 (1.03-1.08) per 1-h reduction below 7 h (log_rr 0.05827, SE 0.01209), and the shortest-vs-reference estimate is RR 1.14 (1.09-1.20); both could plausibly be read as '6 h vs 7 h'. n set to null: the CVD analyses comprise 37 reports (26 in the non-linear analysis) with 58,919 total CVD cases, but no participant count specific to the CVD outcome is reported (3,582,016 participants across all four outcomes). Tier: the scheme has no category for meta-analyses of observational studies, so I assigned T5 on the basis of the underlying primary design (prospective cohorts with self-reported or interview-assessed sleep duration in all 67 included articles). RoB moderate: prospective cohorts only and mostly high NOS scores, but self-reported exposure, substantial heterogeneity for long sleep, and incidence-versus-mortality subgroup differences for CVD.

citation: Jagnani M. Children's Sleep and Human Capital Production. The Review of Economics and Statistics. 2024;106(4):983-996.
target_unit: SD of math score per 10 minutes later sunset
your_quote: TABLE 2.—EFFECT OF LATER SUNSET ON CHILDREN'S MATH SCORES (STANDARD DEVIATIONS) ... Daily sunset time −0.07∗∗∗ −0.11∗∗∗ −0.09∗∗∗ −0.10∗ (10 minutes) (0.01) (0.01) (0.01) (0.05) ... Observations 7,511 7,511 4,589 7,415 || Results. I find a 10-minute delay in sunset time reduces children's math scores by 0.1 standard deviation (SD) (table 2, column 2).
your_note: Took the author's baseline specification, Table 2 column 2 (week-of-year fixed effects, standard errors clustered at the child level), which the Results text cites: -0.11 SD of the standardised math score per 10 minutes later sunset, SE 0.01, 7,511 child-test observations. Negative = worse math performance with later sunset (i.e. with less sleep). DISAGREEMENT RISK: the abstract and text round this to 'roughly 0.1 SD', and the most saturated specification (column 4, child plus week-of-year fixed effects) gives -0.10 with SE 0.05 on 7,415 observations, while the no-controls column gives -0.07 (0.01); an extractor quoting the abstract would report -0.10. Design: this is the reduced-form effect of sunset timing on test scores, identified from cross-district variation in daily sunset within week-of-year, so quasi_experiment / T2 (the paper elsewhere uses sunset as an instrument for sleep, which would be instrumental_variable, but that is a different estimand than the one named here). RoB moderate: credible natural-experiment identification with falsification tests, but observational data, only seven districts (clusters) with wild-cluster-bootstrap inference, and the short-run estimate is potentially partly cumulative.

citation: Illingworth G, Manchanda T, Skripkauskaite S, Fazel M, Waite F. Social jetlag and sleep habits in children and adolescents: Associations with autonomy (bedtime setting and electronics curfew) and electronic media use before sleep. Chronobiology International. 2025;42(1):46-57.
your_quote: The mean social jetlag was 1.88 h (SD = 1.12 h) while actual social jetlag was approximately the same at 1.85 h (SD = 1.17 h).
your_note: Mean absolute social jetlag (difference between weekend and school-night midsleep) in school years 5-13 (typical age 9-18 y) from the 2021 OxWell Student Survey: 1.88 h, equal to the abstract's '1 h 53 min'. SE of the mean = 1.12/sqrt(19,760) = 0.00797. n = 19,760 respondents who reported sleep/wake timing (the gender comparison has df = 18,616, so slightly fewer had complete gender plus SJL data). Alternatives that could be picked instead: 'actual' (signed) social jetlag 1.85 h (SD 1.17), and the age-15 peak of 2.11 h (abstract: 2 h 7 min). RoB na: descriptive mean from a large cross-sectional self-report survey; limitations are measurement (sliding-scale bed/wake times, derived midsleep) and a non-probability school sample rather than bias in an effect estimate.

citation: Gee B, Orchard F, Clarke E, Joy A, Clarke T, Reynolds S. The effect of non-pharmacological sleep interventions on depression symptoms: A meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Sleep Med Rev. 2019 Feb;43:118-128.
your_quote: The subgroup analyses showed that the pooled effect on depression symptoms for these seven studies was large (standardised mean difference = -0.81, 95% CI -1.13, -0.49, p<0.001, k=7) and the statistical heterogeneity among these studies was small (I2=27%, χ2=8.19, df=6, p=0.22).
your_note: Planned subgroup of the seven trials that recruited participants with clinical mental health problems (typically anxiety, depression, PTSD) in addition to sleep difficulties: pooled SMD -0.81 (95% CI -1.13, -0.49). SMD is on the Cohen's-d metric, so no rescaling needed. SE = (-0.49 - (-1.13))/3.92 = 0.16327. Sign: negative = fewer depression symptoms after the sleep intervention, i.e. benefit of better sleep, which is consistent with the task convention that negative indicates the worse outcome under worse/shorter sleep. n set to null: only k = 7 trials is reported for this subgroup; the paper gives participant totals only for the full meta-analysis (5,908 participants, 2,731 randomised to the sleep intervention, 49 trials). Contrast values not matching this target: whole-sample SMD -0.45 (-0.55, -0.36; k = 49) and the no-mental-health-problem subgroup -0.41 (-0.51, -0.31; k = 42). Retrieved the accepted-manuscript PDF via Unpaywall. RoB moderate: pooled RCTs, but mostly self-reported depression outcomes, waitlist/TAU comparators, and a small subgroup with wide CI.

citation: Rupp TL, Wesensten NJ, Balkin TJ. Trait-like vulnerability to total and partial sleep loss. Sleep. 2012;35(8):1163-1172.
target_unit: lapses per PVT (SD, = sqrt of published within-subjects variance component)
your_quote: Table 3 (Variance Components, columns σ2bs (SE) | σ2ws (SE) | ICC | Z | P): PVT lapses | 83.90 (30.62) | 10.45 (3.59) | 0.89 | 2.74 | 0.006
your_note: Within-subjects variance component for PVT lapses is sigma^2_ws = 10.45 (SE 3.59) in Table 3; the target asks for its square root, so value = sqrt(10.45) = 3.2326 lapses per PVT session. SE by the delta method: SE(sqrt(V)) = SE(V)/(2*sqrt(V)) = 3.59/(2*3.2326) = 0.5553. n = 19 volunteers (20 completed, 1 excluded for a positive amphetamine screen). CAVEAT relevant to the target spec: the variance-components model was fitted across BOTH sleep-loss challenges (2 nights of total sleep deprivation and 7 nights of 3 h TIB sleep restriction, order counterbalanced, with fixed effects for order, condition and their interaction), so sigma^2_ws reflects within-subject variability across the TSD and SR conditions rather than the 3-h-TIB restriction alone; the target's exposure description (3 h vs 10 h for 7 days) covers only the SR arm. For reference, the between-subjects component is 83.90 (SE 30.62), whose square root (9.16 lapses) is the paper's index of trait-like interindividual variability and is a plausible alternative extraction. Table 3 is available in PMC only as a table image, so the numbers were read from the image; ICC 0.89 and Z/P values corroborate the row identification.

citation: Kuroda H, Yeung SLA, Fujii R, Iwagami M, Goto A. Investigating the non-linear association between sleep duration and type 2 diabetes: conventional and Mendelian randomization analyses from the UK Biobank. J Diabetes Investig. 2025;16(6):1126-1137.
target_unit: log OR of T2D per unit genetically predicted liability to short sleep
your_quote: Short sleep duration was associated with type 2 diabetes risk for most methods (OR of inverse variance weighting [IVW], 1.12; 95% CI, 1.02–1.23). Conversely, no strong effect of long sleep duration on type 2 diabetes risk were suggested (OR of IVW, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.60–1.07), although the MR Egger estimate was highly uncertain.
your_note: Two-sample MR, inverse-variance-weighted estimate for genetically predicted short sleep duration and type 2 diabetes: OR 1.12 (95% CI 1.02-1.23). log_or = ln(1.12) = 0.11333; SE = (ln(1.23) - ln(1.02))/3.92 = 0.04776. Positive = elevated T2D risk with short sleep, matching the task convention. Scaling detail: 'The original MR estimates were multiplied by loge2 (approximately 0.693) to obtain the change in log odds of diabetes for each two-fold increase in odds of shorter or longer sleep', so the estimate is per doubling of the odds of short sleep (a binary liability), not per hour - consistent with the target unit's 'per unit genetically predicted liability'. Instruments: 23 of 25 short-sleep SNPs retained after harmonisation; SNP-outcome data from DIAGRAM (UK Biobank excluded, to limit sample overlap) and FinnGen, combined by random-effects meta-analysis. n set to null: no combined analytic sample size is given for the two-sample MR; the separate UK Biobank observational and non-linear MR analyses used 385,135 participants with 16,699 incident T2D cases. RoB moderate: MR Egger intercept tests were null (p = 0.29) and negative-control analyses suggested little collider bias, but the exposure is questionnaire-based and coarse, outcomes come from hospital inpatient records (likely under-ascertainment), and the population is European-ancestry only.
